title: Graph Theory Investigation Starter
subject: Graph Theory
summary: A finite-simple-graph scaffold for investigating connectivity, bipartiteness, trees, degree, clique number, and chromatic number.
details: This starter helps an instructor build a graph theory Class around finite simple graphs. It separates definitions that students often conflate, provides hand-checkable examples and boundary cases, and exposes a bounded deterministic palette that can resolve against an exact Graph Theory Study revision.

objectives: Read a finite simple graph from vertices and unordered edges without assuming a drawing is the graph itself.
Distinguish connectivity, bipartiteness, and the tree property with explicit witnesses.
Compute order, size, maximum degree, clique number, and chromatic number on small graphs.
Generate and test bounded conjectures while retaining refuting graphs and exact provenance.

concepts.title: Finite simple graph
concepts.plain_language: A finite simple graph has finitely many vertices and edges joining distinct pairs, with no loops or repeated edges.
concepts.formal_definition: A finite simple graph is G=(V,E), where V is finite and E⊆{{u,v}:u,v∈V and u≠v}.

notation.meaning: the set of unordered two-vertex edges

worked_example.prompt: Describe the graph with V={1,2,3} and E={{1,2},{2,3}}.
steps: Both edges join distinct vertices and neither repeats.
worked_example.conclusion: This is a finite simple path on three vertices.

nonexample.explanation: The edge is a loop, which is excluded from a simple graph.

concepts.title: Connected graph
concepts.plain_language: A graph is connected when every pair of vertices can be joined by a route along edges.
concepts.formal_definition: G is connected when for every u,v∈V(G), there is a path u=v₀,v₁,…,vₖ=v with {vᵢ₋₁,vᵢ}∈E(G) for each i.

notation.meaning: u and v are adjacent when {u,v} is an edge
the ordered vertices of a path

steps: Vertices 1 and 3 are joined by the path 1,2,3.
worked_example.conclusion: Every vertex pair has a path, so the graph is connected.

nonexample.explanation: Vertex 3 has no path to 1 or 2, so the graph is disconnected.

concepts.title: Bipartite graph
concepts.plain_language: A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be split into two groups so every edge crosses between the groups.
concepts.formal_definition: G is bipartite when V(G)=A⊔B for disjoint A,B and every {u,v}∈E(G) has one endpoint in A and one in B.

notation.meaning: a disjoint union of the two vertex parts

worked_example.prompt: Give a bipartition of the path 1-2-3-4.
steps: Put alternating vertices in A={1,3} and B={2,4}.
Each path edge crosses from one part to the other.

nonexample.prompt: The triangle with all three edges.
nonexample.explanation: Alternating two parts around the three-cycle forces the final edge to have both endpoints in one part.

concepts.title: Tree
concepts.plain_language: A tree is a connected graph that contains no closed route returning to its start.
concepts.formal_definition: A finite simple graph G is a tree when G is connected and contains no cycle, equivalently when G is connected and |E(G)|=|V(G)|-1.

worked_example.prompt: Decide whether the path 1-2-3-4 is a tree.
steps: It has four vertices and three edges and contains no cycle.

nonexample.explanation: It is connected but contains a three-cycle, so it is not a tree.

concepts.title: Order
concepts.plain_language: The order of a graph is its number of vertices.
concepts.formal_definition: For a finite graph G=(V,E), order(G)=|V(G)|, the cardinality of its vertex set.

notation.meaning: the cardinality of the vertex set

worked_example.prompt: Find the order of the path 1-2-3-4.

nonexample.prompt: Call the number of edges the order.
nonexample.explanation: Edge count is size; order counts vertices.

concepts.title: Size
concepts.plain_language: The size of a graph counts how many distinct unordered edges it contains.
concepts.formal_definition: For a finite graph G=(V,E), size(G)=|E(G)|, the cardinality of its edge set.

notation.meaning: the cardinality of the edge set

worked_example.prompt: Find the size of the path 1-2-3-4.

nonexample.prompt: Count both {1,2} and {2,1} in a simple graph.
nonexample.explanation: Edges are unordered, so these names describe the same edge once.

concepts.title: Maximum degree
concepts.plain_language: Maximum degree is the largest number of neighbors any one vertex has.

notation.meaning: the number of neighbors of v

nonexample.prompt: Add all vertex degrees and call the result Δ(G).
nonexample.explanation: Δ uses the largest single degree, not their sum.

concepts.title: Clique number
concepts.plain_language: Clique number is the largest number of vertices that are all pairwise adjacent.
concepts.formal_definition: A clique is C⊆V(G) such that every two distinct vertices in C form an edge. The clique number ω(G) is the maximum |C|.

notation.meaning: a set of pairwise adjacent vertices

worked_example.prompt: Find ω for a triangle with a pendant vertex.
steps: The three triangle vertices are pairwise adjacent.
The pendant vertex cannot enlarge that clique.

nonexample.prompt: Treat the path 1-2-3 as a three-vertex clique.
nonexample.explanation: Vertices 1 and 3 are not adjacent, so the whole path is not a clique.

concepts.title: Chromatic number
concepts.plain_language: Chromatic number is the fewest colors needed so adjacent vertices receive different colors.
concepts.formal_definition: A proper k-coloring is c:V(G)→{1,…,k} with c(u)≠c(v) for every {u,v}∈E(G). The chromatic number χ(G) is the least such k.

notation.meaning: the minimum number of colors in a proper coloring

steps: Every pair of triangle vertices is adjacent, so three different colors are necessary.
Assigning one color to each vertex shows three suffice.

nonexample.prompt: Use three colors on a path and conclude its chromatic number is 3.
nonexample.explanation: Chromatic number is a minimum. A nontrivial path can be properly colored with two colors.

object_family.label: Finite simple graphs
object_family.scope: Instructor-approved simple graphs with at most 12 vertices from an exact bound Study revision.
object_family.representation: canonical graph encoding with reconstructible vertex and edge sets
